stages.title: Consumer and producer theory
stages.hook: When your income rises 10% and you buy 15% more restaurant meals but 5% fewer bus tickets, what does that reveal about how you rank goods?
explain: Consumer theory models a person who maximises utility subject to a budget constraint. At the optimum the marginal rate of substitution (MRS, how much of one good the person would give up for another) equals the price ratio: MRS = Px ÷ Py. Equivalently, marginal utility per unit of money is equal across goods: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py.

A price change has two effects. The substitution effect makes the relatively cheaper good more attractive. The income effect changes purchasing power. For normal goods both push quantity in the same direction. For inferior goods the income effect works the other way. Income elasticity of demand = % change in quantity ÷ % change in income: above 1 is a luxury, between 0 and 1 a necessity, below 0 an inferior good.

Producer theory mirrors this. A cost-minimising firm uses inputs so that marginal product per unit of money is equal: MPL ÷ w = MPK ÷ r. Isoquants show combinations of labour and capital giving the same output. These models are idealisations that assume stable preferences and good information.

example.q: A consumer has utility U = x·y, income 120, Px = 2 and Py = 4. Find the optimal bundle.
steps: For U = xy, MRS = y ÷ x; set equal to Px ÷ Py = 0.5, so y = 0.5x.

analogies.home: A household balancing food and transport weighs the extra benefit of each coin spent.
analogies.farm: A farmer shifts to more labour if machines become dearer.
analogies.music: A band weighs extra rehearsal time against extra gigs.
analogies.tech: A phone shopper trades camera quality for battery life at a given price.

stages.mnemonic: Equalise bang per buck: MU/P the same everywhere; MP/price the same for inputs.
terms: The rate at which a consumer will swap one good for another keeping utility constant.
Change in quantity due to change in purchasing power.
Change in quantity due to a change in relative prices.
% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income.

misc.wrong: Consumers literally calculate utility before shopping.
misc.right: The model is 'as if': it predicts behaviour without claiming people compute, and its limits are tested by behavioural evidence.

stages.limits: Preferences are assumed stable and consistent. Behavioural economics shows systematic departures, and the aggregation from individuals to markets adds further assumptions.

questions.q: Why does the 'as if' defence of utility maximisation not prove the model is correct?
questions.model: A model can predict well without people computing utility, but it must be tested against evidence. Behavioural findings show systematic departures, such as inconsistent preferences, so its assumptions hold only in some settings.
questions.why: Predictive success is an empirical question.

doubles

questions.why: The budget line is unchanged, so the optimum is the same (demand is homogeneous of degree zero).

panel.q: A Giffen good would show a rising demand curve. Why are Giffen goods considered rare?
o: The income effect would have to outweigh the substitution effect for a strongly inferior staple
Their demand rises only when the good is cheap, so buyers react in the usual way
They have no price, so they cannot be studied
Substitution effects are always zero for every staple good
panel.why: It requires a very large budget share and strong inferiority.

panel.q: Why does the substitution effect always push quantity demanded the opposite way to price, while the income effect can go either way?
panel.model: When a good gets cheaper relative to others, consumers shift towards it, whatever their income. The income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, so it can reinforce or offset the substitution effect.
panel.why: The sign of the income effect depends on the good type.

panel.q: Why might welfare comparisons using consumer surplus be contested?
o: They depend on willingness to pay, which depends on income
Surplus is not defined for any good, so it cannot be used
Prices are random, so no comparison can be made
Utility is directly observable, so no dispute can arise
panel.why: Dollars from rich and poor are weighted equally in simple surplus measures.

teach.model: A consumer picks the bundle that gives the most utility within her budget. At the best bundle the rate at which she is willing to swap one good for another equals the ratio of their prices. When prices change there is a substitution effect and an income effect. For example, with U = xy, income 120, prices 2 and 4, she buys 30 of x and 15 of y.

points.ask: What is the consumer trying to do?
What condition holds at the optimum?
What happens when a price changes?
Can you give a numerical example?

stages.title: Firm behaviour and industrial organisation
stages.hook: A single seller faces the whole market's demand. How much will it produce, and who loses compared with competition?
explain: A profit-maximising firm chooses output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. A price-taking firm in perfect competition has MR = P, so it produces where P = MC. A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand, so MR is below price: for linear demand P = a − bQ, MR = a − 2bQ. It restricts output and sets a price above MC.

The Lerner index, (P − MC) ÷ P, measures market power. The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) sums the squared market shares (in percentage points) and is used to gauge concentration. In oligopoly, firms' decisions are interdependent; they may compete on quantity (Cournot) or on price (Bertrand), and outcomes lie between monopoly and competition.

Market power is not the same as harm. Dominant firms may be more efficient, innovate or serve markets with large fixed costs. Competition policy weighs possible price increases against efficiency gains and dynamic effects, and economists disagree about how strictly to enforce it.

example.q: Demand is P = 100 − Q and MC = 20 (no fixed cost). Find monopoly output and price, and deadweight loss compared with competition.

analogies.city: A single train line can set fares higher than if many operators competed.
analogies.farm: The only mill in a district can pay farmers less for grain.
analogies.tech: A dominant platform can set high commissions on sellers.
analogies.sport: A league with one broadcaster can charge fans more for coverage.

stages.mnemonic: MR = MC to choose quantity; read the price off the demand curve.
terms: Extra revenue from one more unit sold.

misc.wrong: A monopolist can charge any price it wants.
misc.right: It can pick a point on the demand curve; a higher price cuts sales, so it chooses where MR = MC.

stages.limits: Textbook models assume known demand and costs. In practice potential entry, regulation and innovation affect behaviour, and HHI depends on how the market is defined.

questions.q: A market has a very high HHI. What can be concluded?
o: It signals potential market power, but harm depends on efficiency, entry and behaviour
Consumers are certainly harmed, since the market is concentrated

questions.why: Concentration is a signal, not proof.

panel.q: A firm with high fixed costs and a natural monopoly is regulated with price = marginal cost. What problem does this create?
o: It may make a loss, so subsidy or two-part pricing may be needed
It earns an infinite profit, which regulators must reduce
It raises price above marginal cost, which hurts buyers
It has no costs, so the rule cannot be applied
panel.why: With decreasing average cost, MC is below AC.

panel.q: Why might the threat of entry limit a dominant firm's prices even without regulation?
panel.model: If high prices and profits would attract new entrants, the incumbent may hold prices down to deter them, so a contestable market can behave competitively even with few firms.
panel.why: Contestability restrains market power.

panel.q: In a Cournot duopoly the equilibrium output is usually...
o: between monopoly and perfectly competitive levels
equal to the monopoly level, as firms behave as a single seller
equal to the competitive level, as price falls to marginal cost
zero, since the firms cancel each other's output
panel.why: Firms internalise only part of their effect on price.

teach.model: A monopolist sets output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Because it must cut the price to sell more, marginal revenue is below price, so it produces less and charges more than a competitive market. The lost gains are the deadweight loss. For example, with P = 100 − Q and MC = 20 it picks Q = 40 and P = 60.

stages.title: Macroeconomic modelling
stages.hook: Why can two economists use the same data and the same simple model yet recommend different policies?
explain: Macroeconomic models simplify the economy to study relationships. In the Keynesian cross, income equals planned expenditure: Y = C + I + G with C = a + cY, giving Y = (a + I + G) ÷ (1 − c) and a multiplier of 1 ÷ (1 − c). IS-LM adds money markets; AD-AS adds price levels.

Growth models explain long-run output. In the Solow model with production y = √k, saving s and depreciation plus population growth (n + δ), steady state capital per worker satisfies s√k = (n + δ)k, so k* = (s ÷ (n + δ))². Saving raises the level of income but not the long-run growth rate; sustained growth in income per person needs technological progress.

Models rest on assumptions: how flexible prices are, how forward-looking people are, and what is held constant. Schools of thought (Keynesian, monetarist, new classical, new Keynesian) emphasise different features. The Lucas critique warns that relationships estimated under one policy regime may change when policy changes.

example.q: In a Keynesian cross, C = 100 + 0.8Y, I = 100, G = 100. Find equilibrium Y. Then find k* and y* in a Solow model with y = √k, s = 0.3 and n + δ = 0.1.

analogies.farm: A farm's yield depends on how many tools each worker has, but extra tools help less and less.
analogies.city: A model city map omits many streets to show the main routes.
analogies.music: A score is a model of a performance and leaves out details.
analogies.tech: A flight simulator approximates real conditions but not every factor.

stages.mnemonic: Models are maps: useful because they leave things out, risky when you forget what was left out.

Position where capital per worker and output per worker stay constant.

Ratio of change in output to change in autonomous spending.

misc.wrong: A model with unrealistic assumptions is useless.
misc.right: Simplification is the point, but conclusions must be checked against evidence and the assumptions understood.

stages.limits: Different models can fit the same data. Macro evidence is limited by few observations, shocks that overlap and the inability to run controlled experiments.

questions.q: Explain why economists may disagree on policy even when they use the same data.
questions.model: They may rely on different assumptions about price flexibility, expectations and behaviour, and may weigh goals such as inflation, jobs or equity differently, so the same data can support different conclusions.
questions.why: Both model choice and values matter.

panel.q: Why might multipliers in the data be smaller than in the Keynesian cross?

The cross is exact, so real data must match it
Consumption is constant, so spending cannot respond

panel.q: Why is it hard to test macroeconomic theories?
panel.model: We have one history of each economy and cannot run controlled experiments. Shocks overlap and many variables move together, so isolating causes with limited data is difficult.
panel.why: Identification is a core challenge.

panel.q: A model's prediction fails in a crisis. The best response is to...
o: examine which assumptions failed and revise or combine models
discard all models, since none can be trusted after a failure
ignore the event, as a single case proves nothing
assume the data are wrong, since the model must be right

teach.model: Macro models simplify the economy. In the Keynesian cross, output equals planned spending, so a rise in spending is multiplied by 1 divided by (1 minus the marginal propensity to consume). In the Solow model, saving raises the level of income but long-run growth needs new technology. Models rest on assumptions, so conclusions need testing.

What does Solow say about saving and growth?
What are the limits?

stages.title: Banking and financial systems
stages.hook: A bank holds only a fraction of deposits as cash. Why is that normal, and why can it still be fragile?
explain: Banks perform maturity transformation: they take short-term deposits and make longer-term loans. Their profit comes mainly from net interest income (interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits) and fees. A bank's balance sheet has assets (loans, securities, reserves) and liabilities (deposits, borrowing) plus equity (the owners' capital).

Leverage is assets ÷ equity. High leverage magnifies returns and losses. If a bank has equity of 8% of assets, losses of 8% of assets wipe out its equity. A bank run occurs when many depositors withdraw at once, fearing losses; since assets are not liquid, even a solvent bank can fail. Tools to reduce this include deposit insurance, capital and liquidity requirements, and a central bank acting as lender of last resort.

Regulation involves trade-offs. Stricter rules can reduce crises but may raise the cost of credit; deposit insurance can create moral hazard because depositors and banks take more risk. Economists and policymakers debate how to balance stability, competition and access to finance, including shadow banking and new payment technologies.

example.q: A bank has assets of 1,000, equity of 80, loans of 800 earning 6% and deposits of 700 costing 2%. Find (a) leverage, (b) the asset loss that wipes out equity, (c) net interest income from these loans and deposits.
example.a: Leverage 12.5; an 8% asset loss wipes out equity; net interest income 34

teach.topic: How banks work and why runs happen
teach.model: Banks take short-term deposits and make longer-term loans, earning the difference in interest. They hold only a fraction of deposits as cash, and use a thin layer of owners' equity. If many depositors withdraw at once, a bank can fail even if its loans are good. Insurance, capital rules and central bank lending reduce the risk.

stages.title: Econometrics fundamentals
stages.hook: Cities with more ice cream sales have more drownings. Does ice cream cause drowning? How would an economist find out?
explain: Econometrics uses statistics to estimate relationships in data. In simple regression y = α + βx + ε, ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses the line minimising the sum of squared residuals. The slope is β̂ = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)² and the intercept α̂ = ȳ − β̂x̄. R² measures the share of variation in y explained by the model.

A coefficient is an estimate with uncertainty. The standard error measures its precision; the t-statistic is estimate ÷ standard error, and a large absolute value (roughly above 2) suggests the coefficient is unlikely to be zero by chance. A p-value is the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if the true effect were zero; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

Correlation is not causation. Omitted variables (like summer heat in the ice cream example), reverse causality and measurement error can bias estimates. Researchers use randomised trials, natural experiments, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables and controls to try to identify causal effects. Good practice includes reporting uncertainty and being honest about assumptions.

example.q: Data (x, y): (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 9). Find the OLS slope and intercept, and R².

analogies.farm: Comparing yields on fields that got fertiliser with fields that did not, while checking that soil and rain are similar.
analogies.city: Comparing neighbourhoods before and after a new bus line, with a similar neighbourhood as a benchmark.
analogies.sport: Judging a coach's effect while accounting for the quality of the squad.
analogies.tech: An A/B test of two app designs randomly assigns users.

stages.mnemonic: Fit the line, check the noise, hunt the confounders.

Share of variation in the outcome explained by the model.

stages.limits: Statistical significance is not practical importance, and results depend on model choice. Replication and transparency matter.

panel.q: Why is it risky to run many regressions and report only the significant ones?
panel.model: With many tests, some will look significant by chance alone. Reporting only those overstates the evidence and the results often fail to replicate.
panel.why: Selective reporting inflates false positives.

Errors are zero, so the estimate has no noise
panel.why: Parallel trends lets the control group stand in for the counterfactual.

teach.model: Regression fits a line through data by minimising squared errors, giving a slope that shows how y changes with x on average. Standard errors show uncertainty. But a relationship in data is not automatically causal, because another factor may drive both. Researchers use experiments and careful designs to get closer to causal effects.

Why isn't correlation enough?
How can we get at causes?

stages.title: Game theory
stages.hook: Two rival shops each know that cutting prices wins customers, yet both end up worse off. Why can't they just agree to keep prices high?
explain: Game theory studies strategic interaction, where each player's best choice depends on what others do. A game has players, strategies and payoffs. A dominant strategy is best whatever the others do. A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where no player can gain by changing their own strategy while others keep theirs.

In the prisoner's dilemma, each player's dominant strategy leads to an outcome worse for both than cooperation. Repeated play can sustain cooperation if players value the future enough and can punish defection. In Cournot duopoly with P = 100 − Q and MC = 10, each firm best-responds to the other's quantity: q = (90 − q_other) ÷ 2, giving q = 30 each, P = 40, profit 900 each; if they colluded they would produce a total of 45, with profit 1,012.5 each.

Games can have several equilibria, mixed strategies (randomising) or sequential moves solved by backward induction. Game theory gives insight into pricing, auctions, bargaining and climate agreements, but real people may not play as the theory predicts, and the model depends on assumed payoffs.

example.q: Two firms choose Advertise or Not. Payoffs (A, B) in profit: both Advertise 3,3; A advertises, B not 5,1; A not, B advertises 1,5; neither 4,4. Find the Nash equilibrium.
steps: If B advertises, A gets 3 by advertising and 1 by not: advertise is better. If B does not, A gets 5 versus 4: advertise again.
Advertising is dominant for A, and by symmetry for B.
Equilibrium: both advertise (3,3), although (4,4) would make both better off.
example.a: Both advertise (3,3), the prisoner's dilemma outcome

analogies.sport: Two cyclists in a race each prefer to draft behind the other, causing a standoff.

analogies.city: Two petrol stations cut prices to win customers and both earn less.
analogies.music: Two bands on a bill each want the best slot.

stages.mnemonic: Nash: no regrets given what others do.
terms: A strategy that is best whatever others do.
No player gains by unilaterally changing strategy.
A game where individual incentives produce a worse joint outcome.
Solving a sequential game from the end.

misc.wrong: Nash equilibrium is the best outcome for the players.
misc.right: It is stable, not necessarily efficient. The prisoner's dilemma equilibrium is worse for both than cooperation.

stages.limits: Results depend on assumed payoffs and rationality. Experiments show people often cooperate or reject unfair offers more than the theory predicts.

trip.prompt: Find the payoff matrix and how repeated play changes the outcome.

questions.q: A dominant strategy is one that...
o: is best whatever the others choose
is best only if others cooperate
always gives the highest total payoff
is chosen last
questions.why: It does not depend on others' choices.

questions.q: A Nash equilibrium is...
o: a profile where no player gains by deviating alone
the outcome with the highest total payoff for all players
a draw, in which nobody gains or loses
always unique, so every game has just one
questions.why: It is stable against unilateral changes.

questions.q: Cournot: P = 100 − Q, MC = 10, two identical firms. What is each firm's equilibrium quantity?
With each firm producing 30, what is the market price?
With P = 40, MC = 10 and q = 30, what is each firm's profit?
If the firms colluded and produced the monopoly total Q = 45 (P = 55, MC = 10) and split it equally, what is each firm's profit?
Why is cartel collusion hard to sustain?
o: Each member gains by secretly cheating, so the agreement is unstable
Cartels always earn nothing, so no one joins them
Cheating is impossible, so the problem is something else
Payoffs are identical for every member, so none can gain

questions.q: Match each concept to its description.
Explain how repeated interaction can sustain cooperation in a prisoner's dilemma.
questions.model: If players meet repeatedly, cheating today can be punished in later rounds, and if they value the future enough, the long-run loss from punishment outweighs the short-run gain, so cooperation can be an equilibrium.
questions.why: The shadow of the future disciplines behaviour.

questions.q: In matching pennies (one player wins if coins match, the other if they differ), there is no pure-strategy equilibrium. Optimal play is to...
o: randomise 50-50
always choose heads
always choose tails
alternate predictably
questions.why: Any predictable pattern can be exploited.

panel.q: Experiments show many people reject very unfair offers in the ultimatum game even at a cost to themselves. What does this suggest about the theory?
o: Payoffs may include fairness concerns not captured by money
People are random, so no theory can describe them
The theory is useless and should be dropped
People do not understand money, so they make mistakes
panel.why: Social preferences can alter payoffs.

panel.q: Why might international climate agreements face a prisoner's-dilemma-type problem?
panel.model: Each country bears the cost of cutting emissions but the benefits are shared globally, so each has an incentive to free-ride. Without enforcement or commitments, cooperation is hard to sustain.
panel.why: Shared benefits and private costs create free-riding.

panel.q: Why does the order of moves matter in sequential games?
o: Later movers can respond, and earlier movers can commit, changing outcomes
It never matters who goes first, whatever the game
Only the last player has payoffs, so order is key
Moves are random, so order changes nothing
panel.why: Commitment and information change strategy.

teach.topic: Nash equilibrium and the prisoner's dilemma
teach.model: In game theory each player picks the best action given what others do. A Nash equilibrium is where nobody gains by changing alone. In a prisoner's dilemma each player has a dominant strategy to defect, so both end up worse off than if they cooperated. Repeated play and enforcement can help. For example, two shops cutting prices both lose profit.

points.ask: What makes a situation a game?
What is a Nash equilibrium?
What is the prisoner's dilemma?
How can cooperation be sustained?

stages.title: Public economics
stages.hook: A tax on a polluting product can improve outcomes, yet it also takes money from people. How do economists weigh the two effects?
explain: Public economics studies how governments raise and spend money and the effects on welfare. A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost can correct a negative externality. Tax incidence asks who bears a tax in reality, not who writes the cheque: it depends on relative elasticities, with the less elastic side bearing more.

Governments choose between efficiency and equity. Optimal tax theory balances revenue and distribution against distortions. Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) compares the present value of benefits with costs: NPV = Σ (B_t − C_t) ÷ (1 + r)^t, accepting projects with positive NPV, and the choice of discount rate matters, especially for long-lived projects such as climate action.

Public choice theory notes that governments are made of people with incentives, so policy can be shaped by lobbying or short-term pressure. Economists disagree about the size of government, the efficiency cost of taxation and how much weight to give to equality, which depend on values as well as evidence.

example.q: Demand P = 50 − Q, private supply P = 10 + Q, external cost 8 per unit. Find the market quantity, the socially efficient quantity, the Pigouvian tax and who bears it.
steps: Market: 50 − Q = 10 + Q gives Q = 20, P = 30.
Social cost = 18 + Q: 50 − Q = 18 + Q gives Q = 16. Pigouvian tax = 8.
With the tax: buyers pay 34 and sellers receive 26. Buyers bear 4 and sellers bear 4.
example.a: Market Q = 20; efficient Q = 16; tax 8 split 4 and 4

analogies.home: A household rule that charges a small fee for a shared resource when someone overuses it.
analogies.farm: A fee on water use discourages waste.
analogies.city: Congestion charges make drivers pay for the delay they impose on others.
analogies.nature: A levy on fishing quotas protects fish stocks.

stages.mnemonic: Make the polluter pay the price of the harm; look at who really bears the tax.
terms: A tax equal to the marginal external cost.
Who actually bears the burden of a tax.
Sum of discounted benefits minus costs.

misc.wrong: The person legally required to pay a tax bears its cost.
misc.right: The economic burden depends on elasticities and can fall largely on the other side of the market.

stages.limits: External costs and discount rates are hard to estimate, and the weights on equity differ across people. CBA can undervalue things that are hard to price.

trip.prompt: Find how a Pigouvian tax is shown on a supply and demand diagram.

questions.q: Demand P = 50 − Q and private supply P = 10 + Q. What is the market equilibrium quantity?
The external cost is 8 per unit, so social cost is P = 18 + Q. What is the socially efficient quantity?
With the tax of 8, what price do buyers pay?
With the tax of 8 and Q = 16, what is the tax revenue?
A project costs 1,000 now and gives 400 per year for 3 years. At a 5% discount rate, what is the NPV (nearest whole unit)?
The burden of a tax falls more on the side of the market that is...
o: less elastic
more elastic
larger
poorer by law
questions.why: The less elastic side cannot easily avoid the tax.

questions.q: Raising the discount rate in a CBA of a long-term climate project generally...
o: lowers the present value of future benefits
raises it, since waiting makes the benefits worth more
leaves it unchanged, since benefits are the same sum
makes the costs vanish, so the project looks cheaper
questions.why: Distant benefits are discounted more heavily.

questions.q: Match each concept to its meaning.
Give one reason a discount rate for climate policy is controversial.
questions.model: A high discount rate makes benefits to future generations count for little, a low rate counts them more, so the choice reflects ethical judgments about fairness between generations as well as economics.

questions.q: A government considers a tax whose revenue funds services valued by the poor. A fair assessment includes...
o: efficiency costs, who pays and who benefits
only efficiency costs, since fairness cannot be measured
only the revenue raised, and nothing else
nothing, since taxes are neutral and affect nobody

panel.q: Is it appropriate for economists to claim a policy is 'optimal'?
o: Only given stated objectives and assumptions; different welfare weights give different answers
Always, since economics is a science and gives one best answer
Never, since economists should not talk about policy
Optimal means popular, so it is found by a vote
panel.why: Optimality depends on the objective function.

panel.q: How might lobbying lead to policies that differ from cost-benefit results?
panel.model: Groups with concentrated benefits have strong incentives to lobby, while costs spread across many people attract little opposition, so policies can favour narrow interests over net social benefit.
panel.why: Public choice highlights concentrated benefits and dispersed costs.

panel.q: A Pigouvian tax is set at an estimated external cost that proves too high. The result is...
o: output below the social optimum
output above the social optimum
exactly the optimum
no effect
panel.why: Overtaxing cuts output too far.

teach.model: When a product harms others, a tax equal to the harm makes the producer pay the full social cost, moving output towards the efficient level. Who really bears a tax depends on how sensitive buyers and sellers are to price, not on who sends the money to the government. For example, an 8-coin tax can be shared 4 and 4.

points.ask: What problem does a Pigouvian tax address?
How is the tax set?
Who really pays a tax?
How do we compare costs and benefits over time?

stages.title: Behavioural economics
stages.hook: People often choose the default option on forms, even when changing is free. What does that tell us about how humans really decide?
explain: Behavioural economics uses psychology to understand real decisions. It finds systematic patterns: loss aversion (losses feel bigger than equal gains, often about twice as big), present bias (overweighting rewards now), framing (the same choice described differently changes decisions), anchoring, and a strong pull of defaults and social norms.

Prospect theory describes valuation relative to a reference point, with losses weighing more than gains. Quasi-hyperbolic discounting uses a present-bias factor β below 1 for all future rewards, which can explain procrastination: with β = 0.8, 100 now beats 110 next month (100 vs 88) but 100 in 12 months loses to 110 in 13 months (80 vs 88).

Policy applications include 'nudges' such as automatic enrolment in pensions, which shifts participation without banning options. Critics raise concerns about paternalism, manipulation and whether results scale, and note that people also have bounded rationality, using useful rules of thumb. Debates continue about whether behavioural findings should replace or refine standard models.

example.q: Loss aversion λ = 2: gains count at face value but losses count double. A gamble offers a 50% chance to win 150 and a 50% chance to lose 100. Compare its expected money value with its subjective value.
steps: A loss-averse person may reject a gamble with positive expected money value.
example.a: Expected value +25, subjective value −25, so it may be rejected

analogies.home: A subscription that renews automatically keeps many people paying.
analogies.city: A shop labelled 'Was 100, now 70' anchors you to 100.
analogies.sport: A fan sells a losing bet slowly to avoid 'locking in' a loss.
analogies.tech: Apps set a default setting that most users never change.

terms: Losses weigh more heavily than equal gains.
A change in choice design that steers behaviour without banning options.
How wording or presentation changes choices.

misc.wrong: Behavioural economics shows people are simply irrational.
misc.right: It shows predictable departures from the standard model, and many heuristics work well in everyday settings.

stages.limits: Some behavioural findings have not replicated or vary across cultures, and nudges may have smaller effects at scale. The ethics of nudging are debated.

trip.prompt: Find the value function and what it says about gains and losses.

questions.q: With loss aversion λ = 2, a 50-50 gamble wins 150 or loses 100. What is its subjective value?
Expected money value of the same gamble (win 150 or lose 100 with equal chance)?
A present-biased person with β = 0.8 values 110 next month at what amount today (using only β, no further discounting)?
A pension plan enrols workers automatically unless they opt out, and participation rises sharply. This illustrates...
o: the power of defaults
loss aversion only
comparative advantage
deflation

questions.q: A shop says '20% off' on a price that was raised last week. Which bias is exploited?
o: Anchoring
Diversification
Marginalism
Crowding out
questions.why: The reference price biases perceived value.

questions.q: Which statement about nudges is most accurate?
o: They steer choices without removing options, but raise ethical questions
They ban some options from the list of choices
They always work, since people follow every hint
They are the same as taxes, with another name
questions.why: Nudges preserve choice but can be debated as paternalistic.

questions.q: Match each bias to an example.
pairs: Refusing a fair gamble to avoid losing
Judging a price against an initial number

questions.q: With β = 0.8, 100 now versus 110 next month: she picks 100 now. But 100 in 12 months versus 110 in 13 months: she picks 110. This reversal shows...
o: time inconsistency
rationality, since the person acts the same way at every date
framing, since the questions use different words
risk neutrality, since she treats each sum the same
questions.why: Preferences change as the near date approaches.

questions.q: Give one argument for and one against using nudges in public policy.
questions.model: For: they can improve outcomes at low cost while keeping options open. Against: they may be paternalistic or manipulative, depend on who sets the defaults, and effects may be small at scale.
questions.why: Nudging raises benefits and ethical concerns.

questions.q: If 90% of employees stay in a default savings plan but only 40% join when it is opt-in, the difference is mostly explained by...
o: inertia and framing of the default
different incomes between the two groups of employees
different tax rates between the two plans
different interest rates on the two plans
questions.why: The plan is identical; the choice architecture differs.

panel.q: If people make predictable mistakes, does that justify more government paternalism?
o: Not automatically: officials are also fallible and values about autonomy differ
Yes, always, since any mistake justifies more control
No, never, since mistakes cannot be predicted
Mistakes do not exist, since people always choose well
panel.why: The case depends on evidence and values.

panel.q: Why might a behavioural finding from a laboratory fail to scale to a real market?
panel.model: Lab samples and low stakes differ from real markets, where experience, competition and higher incentives can reduce biases, and results may vary across contexts and cultures.
panel.why: External validity is not guaranteed.

panel.q: Standard and behavioural economics are best viewed as...
o: complementary approaches whose usefulness depends on the question
enemies, so that only one can be right
identical, so there is no difference between them
irrelevant to each other, with no shared ideas
panel.why: Each captures different aspects of behaviour.

teach.model: Behavioural economics shows people do not always decide like the textbook consumer. They dislike losses more than they like equal gains, favour rewards now, and stick with defaults. Policymakers can use nudges such as automatic enrolment in savings plans. For example, a plan with auto-enrolment can have 90% participation instead of 40%.

points.ask: What is loss aversion?
What is present bias?
What is a nudge?
Is nudging always fine?

stages.title: Economic policy analysis
stages.hook: A government wants to know whether a job-training scheme actually worked. How can it separate the scheme's effect from what would have happened anyway?
explain: Policy analysis asks: what is the problem, what are the options, what are the likely effects, and who gains and loses? Tools include cost-benefit analysis, cost-effectiveness analysis (cost per unit of outcome), distributional analysis, and sensitivity analysis, which tests how results change if assumptions change.

Evaluation needs a counterfactual: what would have happened without the policy. Difference-in-differences compares the change in the treated group with the change in a comparison group. If treated earnings rose from 50 to 62 and comparison earnings from 48 to 54, the estimated effect is (62 − 50) − (54 − 48) = 6, assuming parallel trends.

Good analysis separates facts from values, states uncertainty, and considers unintended consequences and implementation. Different people may rank the same options differently, because they weight efficiency, equity, liberty or risk differently. The analyst's role is to make trade-offs transparent, not to hide value judgements behind numbers.

example.q: Programme A costs 2,000,000 zeds and gains 500 life-years of healthy living. Programme B costs 3,000,000 and gains 600. Compare cost-effectiveness, and compute the incremental cost per extra life-year of B over A.
example.a: A is 4,000, B is 5,000; B's extra years cost 10,000 each

analogies.farm: Testing a new seed on some fields and comparing with similar untreated fields.
analogies.city: Comparing a district that got a new bus line with a similar one that did not.
analogies.sport: Judging a training method by comparing improvement with a matched team.
analogies.tech: An A/B test of a new design on random users.

stages.mnemonic: Define, compare options, estimate, weigh, and be honest about doubts.
terms: What would have happened without the policy.
Cost per unit of outcome achieved.
Testing how results change with assumptions.
Comparing changes over time between treated and comparison groups.

misc.wrong: If an outcome improves after a policy, the policy caused it.
misc.right: Other factors may have changed too. Evaluation needs a credible comparison.

stages.limits: Even good evaluations rest on assumptions, and results from one place may not carry over. Distributional and ethical judgements cannot be decided by data alone.

trip.prompt: Find an applied example and the parallel trends assumption.

questions.q: Treated earnings rose from 50 to 62; comparison earnings rose from 48 to 54. What is the difference-in-differences estimate?
A programme costs 900,000 zeds and prevents 300 hospital stays. What is the cost per stay prevented?
Programme A: 2,000,000 for 500 life-years. Programme B: 3,000,000 for 600. What is B's incremental cost per extra life-year over A?
The counterfactual is...
o: what would have happened without the policy
the policy's budget for the year
the policy's goal, as set by its authors
the political opposition to the policy

questions.q: Sensitivity analysis is used to...
o: see how results change if assumptions change
hide uncertainty from readers of the report
raise the budget of the project
remove the policy from the debate

questions.q: Cost-effectiveness analysis differs from cost-benefit analysis because it...
o: measures outcomes in natural units rather than money
ignores costs and looks only at outcomes
values only the profits that a project earns
needs no comparison between different options
questions.why: It avoids putting money values on outcomes like life-years.

questions.q: Match each tool to its purpose.
questions.why: A toolkit rather than a single method.

questions.q: A city's crime fell after it introduced a new policy. List two other explanations that should be ruled out before crediting the policy.
questions.model: Crime may have been falling anyway or in many other cities, or other changes such as the economy, policing or reporting may explain it, or it could be regression to the mean after an unusual peak. A comparison group helps rule these out.

questions.q: Two policies have the same net benefit but one helps the poorest more. What is the best analytic response?
o: Report the distributional difference and let decision-makers weigh it
Ignore the difference, since net benefit is the same
Choose randomly between them, as they are equal
Say the data decides, so there is no need for a judgement
questions.why: Distribution is a value-laden dimension to make transparent.

questions.q: A pilot works in one town. Why be cautious about rolling it out nationally?
o: Context, scale and implementation may change the results
Pilots are always accurate, so nothing will change
Towns are identical, so a result in one holds in all
Costs vanish at scale, so the rollout will be cheap

panel.q: An analyst presents one number as 'the' effect of a policy. What is missing?
o: A range or confidence interval and assumptions
Nothing, since one number is clear enough on its own
More decimal places, which would make it more exact
A shorter report, which would be easier to read
panel.why: Transparent uncertainty is part of good practice.

panel.q: Why can a policy with positive net benefits still be politically or ethically contested?
panel.model: Net benefits can hide that some groups lose while others gain, and people differ on fairness, rights and how to weigh gains and losses, so positive net benefit alone does not settle the decision.
panel.why: Efficiency is not the only criterion.

panel.q: Which is the best description of an analyst's role in a contested policy debate?
o: Make assumptions, evidence and trade-offs transparent
Declare a winner using only the models, and nothing else
Avoid giving any numbers, so no one can dispute them
Hide the uncertainty, so the advice sounds firm
panel.why: Transparency supports informed democratic choice.

teach.model: To judge a policy you compare what happened with what would have happened without it. Difference-in-differences compares the change in a treated group with the change in a similar untreated group. Analysts use tools such as cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness, test assumptions and show who gains and loses. For example, earnings up 12 for the treated and 6 for the comparison group gives an effect of 6.

points.ask: What do we compare against?
How can we estimate the effect?
What tools help weigh the options?
What can data not decide?
